title: AccessiSound: ESP32-S3 Assistive Device
desc: An ESP32-S3 assistive device that recognizes speech and surrounding sounds and gives real-time descriptions to support accessibility. Three real versions: a hackathon prototype, a custom home rebuild, and a gift version with kitchen object recognition that a friend still uses every day.

detail.body:
Spring 2026 · Embedded ML · Accessibility · ESP32-S3

View the full project, code, and documentation: https://github.com/jackpham-rgb/accessisound-esp32s3

[SECTION: What this is]

An assistive device built around an ESP32-S3 that listens to the room, recognizes speech and surrounding sounds, and gives real-time descriptions to support accessibility. It has three real versions, and the kitchen object recognition device I used to list as a separate project is the third one.

[SECTION: The three versions]

[IMAGE: assets/img/accessisound-v1-soda-hacks.jpg | Presenting v1 at SoDA Hacks, holding the ESP32-S3-BOX-3]

v1, March 7, 2026: built at SoDA Hacks at UC Berkeley, my first hackathon, on an ESP32-S3-BOX-3 dev kit that CSUA lent out for the event. I trained the system using basic inputs, online datasets, and CSUA HPC resources. Its physical form is the off-the-shelf dev kit, not an enclosure I designed.

v2: after the hackathon I bought my own ESP32-S3 board and parts and rebuilt it at home, with an ESP32-CAM, a 1.54 inch ST7789 display, a microphone, a USB-C charging circuit and a LiPo battery, in a custom enclosure that ended up looking like a vintage Macintosh 128K. I have no photo of the finished unit, so the repo includes a Fusion 360 reconstruction of the enclosure, layout and wiring, with STL files for printing.

v2.5: built while moving out of the dorm for summer break and adapted for a friend whose family has hearing and visual impairments. I added kitchen object recognition through the ESP32-CAM and a mochi character animation on the display to make it feel friendlier. I gave it to him as a thank you for helping me brainstorm the original hackathon idea, and he still uses it every day in his dorm kitchen.

[IMAGE: assets/img/accessisound-v2-model.png | Even though there is no photo of the physical v2 unit, this picture accurately represents the enclosure model made in Autodesk Fusion]

[IMAGE: assets/img/accessisound-v2-internals.png | Inside the model: display, camera, microphone, DevKit, driver board, charger and battery, with every wire drawn]

[SECTION: Hardware layout and wiring]

v2 is built from off-the-shelf breakout modules wired point to point, not a custom PCB, so the useful drawing is a wiring diagram rather than a board layout. It shows the display, ESP32-CAM, INMP441 microphone, driver board, charger and battery, and every connection between them. Signal colors are unique per line, and the power path runs LiPo, TP4056 USB-C charger, 5 V boost converter, then the DevKit's 5V pin.

[IMAGE: assets/img/accessisound-v2-wiring.png | v2 wiring diagram. The display is a photo of the real module, the other parts are renders from the Fusion model]

[SECTION: How the sound recognition works]

Each 32 ms slice of audio becomes 13 MFCC features (pre-emphasis, Hamming window, power spectrum, 26 mel filters, log, DCT). Thirty-two slices form a 0.53 second window that goes into a small CNN with about 7,400 parameters, and the device alerts when the top guess reaches 72 percent confidence. The repo includes a Python visualization of every step, checked against the firmware's own C++ code.

[IMAGE: assets/img/accessisound-pipeline-steps.png | One 32 ms frame through pre-emphasis, Hamming window, power spectrum, mel filterbank, log and DCT to 13 MFCCs]

[IMAGE: assets/img/accessisound-pipeline-features.png | The same processing over a whole clip. The cyan box is the 32-frame window the CNN sees]

[SECTION: What broke]

The firmware and the training script turned out to compute different features. Training used librosa's MFCC squeezed over a 5 second clip, while the firmware runs a sliding window with pre-emphasis, an 80 Hz mel floor and different normalization. I found this by rewriting the firmware's math in NumPy and compiling the real C++ header to compare the two. On the same audio they agree only partly (mean correlation 0.78, worst coefficient 0.39), so a model trained by the script and run on the device has not been checked end to end. Fixing that is the next step.

[IMAGE: assets/img/accessisound-train-vs-firmware.png | Firmware MFCC (left) against the training MFCC (middle), with per-coefficient correlation (right)]

[SECTION: Honesty line]

The model in the repo is a proof of concept trained on stand-in sounds from the ESC-50 dataset (about 47 to 53 percent test accuracy across 5 classes, where chance is 20 percent). The repo has the sound-recognition code but not yet the camera or animation code from v2.5.
detail.status: v1 presented at SoDA Hacks (March 7, 2026). v2 rebuilt with a custom enclosure. v2.5 delivered to a friend and in daily use.
